title: Lab 1 Report
text: In this lab, a development board was built and programmed using SystemVerilog. This lab focused on using SystemVerilog to program the FPGA using switches, LEDs, and a seven-segment display. The goals were to test out the assembled development board, practice programming in SystemVerilog, and to gain experience in building, assembling, testing, and debugging circuits.

title: Lab 1 Report
text: In this lab, a development board was built and programmed using SystemVerilog. This lab focused on using SystemVerilog to program the FPGA using switches, LEDs, and a seven-segment display. The goals were to test out the assembled development board, practice programming in SystemVerilog, and to gain experience in building, assembling, testing, and debugging circuits.

title: Lab 1 Report
text:
Design and Testing Methodology

Development Board Assembly
The development board was assembled according to the instructions provided in the lab manual as well as in reference to the E155 Development Board BOM. The board was then tested using the provided test programs.


FPGA Design
The FPGA was designed using three modules written in SystemVerilog: the top level module, the switch-to-seven-segment logic module, and the counter logic module.
The top level module was responsible for instantiating the other two modules and the switch-to-LED logic which was written using XOR and AND gates based on the truth tables.
The switch-to-seven-segment logic module was responsible for taking the input from the switches and outputting the corresponding signals to the seven-segment display. Combinational logic was used to implement each combination of the four switches to display the correct segment patterns
The counter logic module was responsible for using sequential logic to make an led blink at 2.4 Hz based on the 48 MHz internal HSOSC clock. The calculations used to divide the high frequency clock signal down to achieve the desired frequency are shown in Figure 1.






NoteMaximum Count Value Calculation






Figure 1: Calculations to find the maximum count value



There was also an enable and reset input implemented into the code.


Testbench Design
Testbenches were created for each of the three modules to verify that the design was functioning as expected. The submodule testbenches used assertions to check that the output of each module matched the expected output for a given input with the 7-segment module covering all input-output pairs and the counter showing that reset, enable, and max count features all worked correctly. The top level module testbench was used to verify that the submodules were connected correctly, the HSOSC worked, and that the switch-to-LED logic was functioning as expected.


Hardware Testing
The 7-segment display circuit was built and assigned GPIO pins along with a current-limiting resistor which was calculated in Figure 2.

The design accomplished all of the design objectives.

title: Lab 1 Report
text:
Conclusion
The design succesfully blinked an LED at 2.4 Hz, displayed the correct output on the 7-segment display based on the input from the switches, and displayed the correct output on the LEDs based on the input from the switches. I spent a total of around 30 hours working on this lab.

title: Week 1 Reflections
text: In this lab we assembled a development board as well as tested out the MCU and FPGA boards. However, the main focus of the lab was to program the FPGA using SystemVerilog. We wrote SystemVerilog code to control the switches, LEDs, and 7-segment display to ensure the board was operational. The programs used were Lattice Radiant (which included QuestaSim) for FPGA as well as a little bit of SEGGER Embedded Studio when testing the MCU. The lab was a succes and we were able to successfully program the FPGA to meet the specifications.

title: Week 1 Reflections
text:
Reflections on Lab
This lab was a great introduction to the course and it was a beneficial experience to learn how to assemble the development board–specifically learning how to solder SMT components and learning how to use solder paste. The tutorials were very beneficial in terms of refreshing my memory on topics as well as teaching me how to use new software. Personally, I found the videos most helpful as following along made the process easier.One downside was that following the instructions while clicking through all the different links and tutorials was a bit confusing. I think it would be beneficial to create an organized list of all the links and tutorials that are needed on a side bar to make locating the resources easier. There were some issues with the connecting the board to program as well as with the software programs themselves, but overall I thought the lab was very detailed and informative. I think in the future I need to first comprehensively read over the lab to try and understand the goals at hand and create a plan of action before diving into the lab. I think this will help me to be more efficient and organized in my work. Due to learning to use new tools, board soldering, and refreshing old topics, this lab took longer taking me around 30 hours.
